# Introduction

In this Final Project, I am going to be using a dataset I found on Basketball Reference: [2025-26 NBA Player Stats: Totals](https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_2026_per_minute.html). The dataset features data from the 2025-2026 NBA season. Note that I am interested in predicting the number of minutes played and, since the website would only allow me to retrieve the top 500 players, I sorted by that variable before exporting the file.

A few notes to make on the data: First, I'm interested in what is more likely to earn a player playing time but I wanted to control for injuries so I created a column in the dataset which calculated my actual response variable: minutes played per game (`MPG`). Next, there were "missing" values in the 3 point percentage column (`3P%`) that reflected players that didn't attempt a 3 point shot (players who attempted at least one, but didn't make any, already had a value of `0` here). I added `0`'s in the places with missing cells, but I plan on using the `3P` column (made 3 point shots per 36 minutes played) so it should not make a difference in my analysis. Finally, I chose to export the data on a per 36 minutes basis, as cumulative total statistics will be heavily influenced by total minutes played.

There are obviously a lot of player statistics that get tracked but I am going to focus on the following predictor variables (again, all measured per 36 minutes played): three point shots made (`3P`), free throws made (`FT`), total rebounds (`TRB`), assists(`AST`), steals (`STL`), blocks (`BLK`), turnovers (`TOV`), personal fouls (`PF`), and points (`PTS`). Note that some of these are often combined in the analysis of NBA players (for instance, often a player's assist to turnover ratio or "stocks" [steals+blocks]) is reported, but I thought combining these might deprive the model of some information, so I left them separate. 

# Reading in data, setting up libraries

Next, I will read in the data set and load the libraries I'll need for the modeling process. 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# Load packages for data preparation, visualization, and modeling
library(lubridate)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidymodels)

#Create data tibble

min_played<-read_csv("../2025-26_NBA_Player_Stats_Per_36.csv")

min_played
```

Note that there there was very little pre-processing that needed to be done, and it was accomplished before reading the data in. 

Another important thing to mention is that we're dealing with numeric variables across the board here, and all the columns are already formatted properly. 

## Splitting the data

Next up, I'll set a seed (one I'm partial to, $\tau$), and split the data for modeling purposes (a 70/30 split, as requested). I choose to stratify the data by position, as the roles these players take on during the game can vary wildly. 

```{r}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(6.28)

# Split data into training and test sets
mp_split <- initial_split(
  min_played, 
  prop = 0.7,
  strata = Pos
)

# Isolate training and test sets

mp_train <- training(mp_split)
mp_test <- testing(mp_split)

# verify my 70/30 split
nrow(mp_train)/nrow(min_played)
nrow(mp_test)/nrow(min_played)
```
Pretty good!
